prime.problem: Training needs P a second time, in the backward pass. Keeping it costs 4.29 GB per layer for Llama-3.1-8B at 8k (137 GB for 32 layers, more than an H100 holds), and the usual fix, checkpointing, makes every step slower.
prime.fits: Card 3 of 3 on FlashAttention. Card I introduced recomputation in one sentence; this card derives the backward pass that uses it (Algorithm 4) and then shows what the speed and memory bought: faster training, longer context, and Path-X.
expect: dV = PᵀdO, dP = dO Vᵀ, dS = P∘(dP − D)
dK, dV on chip, dQ read-modify-written
prime.goal: Explain how the backward pass avoids storing P and the N-length row sum, and read the paper's results as memory-limited vs time-limited wins.

attend: The softmax gradient needs a sum over a whole row of N entries. What identity turns it into a dot product of length d that is already in memory?
Which gradients can accumulate in SRAM for a whole K, V column, and which one must go back to HBM at every step? Why the difference?
Rabe & Staats also tile and recompute. What single difference in goal makes FlashAttention faster while theirs is about the same speed as standard attention?
In Table 11, FlashAttention's memory doubles per doubling of N while its time quadruples. What does that say about which limit it removed?
Why did the long-context results (Path-X, Path-256) depend on memory more than on speed?

must: Backward needs P for dV and dS → storing it is N×N per head (4.29 GB per layer at 8k) → store only (m, ℓ) per row and rebuild each tile of P on chip as exp(S − m)/ℓ → +13% FLOPs, 9× fewer bytes → the backward pass gets faster and smaller
The softmax Jacobian needs Σ_j P_ij·dP_ij over a whole row → since o_i = Σ_j P_ij v_j, that equals do_iᵀo_i → D_i is a length-d dot product computed once → no N-length row has to fit in SRAM

Memory becomes linear in N (209 → 418 → 836 MB per doubling) → sequences that ran out of memory now fit (PyTorch OOM at 8k on 40 GB) → but FLOPs stay O(N²), so time still quadruples per doubling → long context became possible, not cheap
elevated: Outer loop over K, V columns → dK_j, dV_j depend only on column j and stay in SRAM → dQ_i collects from every column → read-modify-write in HBM each step (FA2 later turns this into atomic adds when it parallelizes)
reference: the dropout RNG-state trick (regenerate Z per tile)
the per-benchmark tables (BERT 17.4 min, GPT-2 days, LRA accuracies)

compress.prompt: From memory, write the backward pass as five lines (dV, dP, D, dS, dQ/dK) and mark which matrices are N×N and never stored. Then one sentence on why training memory stopped being quadratic.
checklist: dV = PᵀdO; dP = dO Vᵀ; D_i = do_iᵀo_i; dS = P∘(dP − D); dQ = dS K, dK = dSᵀQ
P, dP and dS are N×N per head and exist only one tile at a time in SRAM
P is rebuilt from the stored m and ℓ
the stored state is 2 numbers per row, so memory grows linearly in N

retrieve.q: Explain why FlashAttention's backward pass is faster than storing P, even though it does more arithmetic.
answer: storing P means writing and re-reading N×N elements through HBM, which is memory-bound
recomputing P tile by tile costs extra matmul FLOPs, which the GPU has to spare
on GPT-2 medium: 75.2 vs 66.6 GFLOPs, 4.4 vs 40.3 GB, 7.3 vs 41.7 ms

retrieve.q: Walk through one inner step of Algorithm 4: what is loaded, what is recomputed, which gradients update where?
answer: load Q_i, O_i, dO_i, dQ_i, m_i, ℓ_i (and D_i) for the current row block; K_j, V_j are already on chip
recompute S_ij = Q_i K_jᵀ and P_ij from m, ℓ
dV_j += PᵀdO_i and dK_j += dSᵀQ_i accumulate in SRAM
dQ_i += dS K_j is written back to HBM

retrieve.q: Whole-layer checkpointing and FlashAttention's recomputation both trade FLOPs for memory. Why does one slow training down and the other speed it up?
answer: whole-layer checkpointing reruns every FLOP of the layer and still builds N×N in HBM during the rerun
FlashAttention recomputes only S and P, on chip, and never writes them
so it saves traffic as well as memory; checkpointing saves memory only

compare.q: FA2's backward keeps one number per row instead of FA1's two. What is that number, what does it save per score, and what does it not change?
answer: the logsumexp L = m + log ℓ
P = exp(S − L) takes 2 ops per score instead of 3 (exp(S − m)/ℓ)
the IO bound, the loop structure and dQ's read-modify-write are unchanged

compare.q: Course 7 treats activation checkpointing as a general training dial. How is FlashAttention's recomputation a special case, and why is it one you never turn off?
answer: both drop stored activations and recompute them in backward
FlashAttention targets the one quadratic activation (P) and recomputes it where it is cheap: on chip, inside the kernel
it is faster as well as smaller, so there is no trade-off to tune

predict.q: Prefill runs only the forward pass, so there is no backward. Does FlashAttention still help prefill of an 8,192-token prompt on Llama-3.1-8B, and does it help the decode steps that follow? Commit first.
predict.answer: It helps prefill: the forward pass still has an N×N score matrix per head (4.29 GB of P per layer at 8k, just transient), and the forward kernel keeps it on chip. It doesn't help decode: each decode step has one query row against the KV cache, so there's no N×N matrix to avoid, and the step is bound by reading the cache (≈ 4 FLOPs/byte with GQA-4).

apply.task: Two checks. (1) In numpy, build random P (softmax rows), V and dO for N = 6, d = 4. Compute Σ_j P_ij·dP_ij with dP = dO Vᵀ, and separately do_iᵀo_i with O = PV. (2) Extend the card's memory table to a 16,384-token training sequence on Llama-3.1-8B (32 heads, 32 layers): P per layer in BF16, P for all layers, (m, ℓ) per layer in FP32, and the ratio.
apply.done: Your two row-sum vectors agree to about 1e-15, and you have four memory numbers with their arithmetic.
apply.hint: The identity holds because o_i = Σ_j P_ij v_j, so Σ_j P_ij (do_i·v_j) = do_i·o_i. Memory at 16k: 32 × 16,384² × 2 B = 17.18 GB per layer; × 32 = 550 GB; 2 × 32 × 16,384 × 4 B = 4.19 MB; ratio N/4 = 4,096× (our arithmetic).
